questions.question: Where does the library have nothing for me?
Why is correction required?
questions.answer: The published interaction model gives the person three responses: confirm, correct the interpretation, or defer. Take correction away and the other two collapse into one, because the engineer can say yes or say nothing. At 03:00 with a service degrading they say yes.

questions.question: What if nobody is on call at all?

recommendation.head: Escalate rather than stall.
recommendation.why: Your actions cannot be undone and a person finds out afterwards. Holding forever means the incident sits there until morning. Escalating keeps a person in it without the agent acting on a reading nobody checked. The pattern itself does not settle this: its interaction model says nothing irreversible happens until you respond, and stops there. So whichever you pick is your decision, recorded as one.
recommendation.cites: signal-to-intent-handshake.interactionModel defines the three responses but no no-answer default, so this is recorded as a scenario decision, not as a pattern element.

questions.question: Could we use Authority Gradient instead?

recommendation.head: Run both, but the library does not back that for you.
recommendation.why: This pattern asks in the moment. Authority Gradient sets what each agent may do on its own, area by area, in advance, so routine actions never wake anyone. Those read as complementary, and with a person out of the loop I would want the gradient carrying the routine and the handshake catching what falls outside it. Be clear about the sourcing though: the library records no relationship between these two. What it does record is that this pattern pairs with Convergence Point, agent-to-human before acting against agent-to-agent after converging. Composition between this and Authority Gradient is your judgement, not a finding.
recommendation.cites: signal-to-intent-handshake.pairsWith is convergence-point; its note explains the sibling relationship. No pattern in the library declares composesWith.

refusal.head: I am not going to do that here.
refusal.why: Correction is one of the three responses the published interaction model defines. Take it away and confirm-or-defer is the whole surface, which makes this a notification the engineer waves through rather than a handshake. You are out of the loop, so if triage's read is wrong nothing else catches it before the action lands. Removing it is a decision for the record with a reason on it, not a quiet edit. questions.question: Why does the old belief matter?
questions.answer: Because things were already done on it. Deploy scaled replicas and paused a job on a reading that turned out to be wrong. The pattern keeps the superseded belief next to the one that displaced it, with attribution for which agent held which, so the person sees a new conclusion and a reason to go back over what was done on the old one.
questions.cites: memory-commitment-review.interactionModel: superseded beliefs appear with their superseding belief and attribution is preserved.

questions.question: How should the person be able to respond?

recommendation.head: Acknowledge, and leave what was already done visible.
recommendation.why: The pattern gives exactly three choices at the commitment boundary: acknowledge the belief, restore it if the update was wrong, or revoke it so it never reaches long-term memory. Restoring is the honest choice when a revision is uncertain, but confidence went up here, not down. Revoking loses the fact that the agent was wrong once, which is the part worth keeping.
recommendation.cites: memory-commitment-review.interactionModel, and the three choices as lib/memory-commitment-data.ts labels them.
